transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-22 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~52m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (Umbria Head of Security), Liam Porter (Platform Eng), Sofia Mendes (Compliance)
Linkouts: shared deck: drive.redwood/umbria-kms, runbook draft: drive.redwood/umbria-kms-runbook, SOC2 redacted: drive.redwood/soc2-umbria-redwood

Auto-generated summary: discussed encrypted logging patterns, KMS access flows, BYOK/HSM expectations, and SSO/RBAC mapping. Agreed to POC and follow-up docs.

00:00 Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we've got about 50 minutes, i'll hand off to diego to outline what we'll go over then we can jump into questions
00:18 Diego: yeah thanks maya, quick agenda — encrypted logs at rest and in transit, how redwood's KMS/connector supports customer keys, HSM integration patterns, and the RBAC/SSO story for tenant isolation. we'll also cover audit trails and SIEM ingestion.
00:45 Aisha: sounds good, we mainly want to make sure logs that contain pii get encrypted with our keys and that the audit chain is tamper-evident, also residency — EU only.
01:05 Diego: absolutely, so twofast points — transport encryption is TLS 1.3, mutual TLS for the private deploy scenarios, and at rest we encrypt with per-tenant envelope keys. by default those are managed by redwood KMS but we support BYOK where you keep the root/wrapping keys in your HSM (PKCS11 or cloud HSM) and we only get wrapped keys.
01:38 Liam: quick clar — when you say "per-tenant envelope" is that per-customer per-environment or per-route? we're trying to map to our multi-tenant event streaming.
01:52 Diego: good q — it's per-tenant (per Umbria account) by default; you can opt for per-route if you want stronger separation for specific data types. there is an overhead on key count but we have key caching and prefix caching to reduce cost.
02:10 Aisha: what's the KMS call pattern? do you see a tok/sec line that will blow up our HSM? we need to understand throughput and latencies — our HSM provider charges for ops.
02:30 Diego: fair — we do envelope encryption pattern: leaf data keys are generated locally in the service and then wrapped with customer root key. the calls to the HSM are for wrap/unwrap and for key material import/export during rotation. runtime path avoids HSM on every token via auditable cache and KMS token TTLs. for high-throughput logging we recommend local DEKs (data encryption keys) with periodic rotation and a short TTL for the cache to balance security and cost.
03:05 Sofia: and the audit trail — we need immutable logs with signed integrity proof for SOC2 and forensics. do you provide signed audit events?
03:20 Diego: current approach — all audit events are write-once in our append-only store. we can optionally sign batches with a HSM-stored signing key (if you're BYOK you can keep signing key in your HSM). that produces a cryptographic proof chain; we'll include an example of the signed log format in the runbook.
03:42 Aisha: ok that'd help, and for SIEM ingestion we want logs to be encrypted in transit to our collector and decrypted only inside our network. can we push encrypted blobs that we then decrypt locally?
04:00 Diego: yes — we support push of encrypted log blobs over mTLS and SFTP endpoints for private deploys. for hosted customers we support an encrypted delivery to a customer-owned log collector (e.g., a TLS endpoint inside their VPC) or to object storage with SSE-C where you manage the key.
04:32 Liam: if we use SSE-C or our own HSM key, what about lifecycle and rotation? how do you handle rewrap when keys are rotated?
04:45 Diego: rewrap can be done in two ways: an online rewrap job that fetches and rewraps keys (requires short downtime for affected objects) or lazy rewrap where objects are rewrapped on access. for logs we recommend lazy rewrap to avoid mass IO. both approaches are documented.
05:10 Maya: aisha — for compliance, are you expecting Redwood to host the root key or you want full custody?
05:22 Aisha: prefer full custody if possible. procurement will want BYOK and an attestation that keys never leave our HSM.
05:34 Diego: BYOK with HSM is supported. we use a wrap/unwrap design where your root key stays in your HSM and we only store wrapped DEKs. you can require attestation/remote attestation during onboarding and we support hardware-backed attestation flows for some vendors.
05:56 Sofia: do you support offline key import or only remote provisioning? we are sometimes air-gapped for high-sensitivity environments.
06:10 Diego: for private/on-prem deployments we support offline import via PKCS#12 with HSM-backed import tooling and an operator-run key ceremony. we'll include the runbook section on key ceremony procedures.
06:35 Aisha: SSO — how do we map Okta groups to Redwood roles? we need separation of duties: ops people can view logs but only security can unseal rewrap operations.
06:52 Maya: we map SAML attributes to RBAC roles. you can have fine-grained roles (log_viewer, key_admin, rewrap_operator). we also support step-up auth for key operations.
07:10 Liam: is there an API or UI control for temporary elevation? our execs want ephemeral access for incident response.
07:22 Diego: yes, there is a temporary role-assumption flow backed by audited approval. that flow generates an ephemeral token tied to an audit entry and email approvals if you want.
07:40 Aisha: audit logs retention — we need 7 years for certain records. do you store logs long-term, or do we pull them into our own archive?
07:56 Diego: we store logs by default for 90 days, but customers can configure long-term retention by exporting to customer-owned object storage (we recommend encrypted buckets inside EU regions). for regulatory long-tail retention we recommend export to the customer's archive; we can automate that export.
08:20 Sofia: data residency — Umbria EU requirement is strict; redwood hosted region selection is fine if processors remain inside eu-central or eu-west. do you have controls to pin tenants to region?
08:38 Maya: yes you can pin model serving and storage to specific regions and restrict cross-region fallbacks. for Dedicated/Private we can guarantee regional isolation.
08:52 Aisha: regarding signed logs and chain verification, can we get a daily signed hash snapshot? for our auditors daily hashes are easier.
09:05 Diego: absolutely — we can produce daily signed manifests with the HSM signing key. if you hold the signing key we can generate a signed counter-snapshot and you verify offline.
09:18 Liam: network-level details — do you support private connectivity and direct peering? our egress policy requires private links from vendors.
09:30 Maya: for Dedicated we support VPC peering, private link equivalents, and customer-managed VPN. Private deployments can be fully air-gapped.
09:42 Aisha: pen test and third-party attestations — do you provide raw logs for auditors to validate?
09:54 Maya: We can provide redacted logs and a forensics package. raw logs are sensitive but we have an established process to grant read-only auditor access under NDA; we also provide SOC2 report and penetration test summary.
10:10 Sofia: curious on fallback behavior — if HSM is unavailable, do you have a fail-closed or fail-open model for decryption?
10:24 Diego: default is fail-closed for key material operations where security is critical; for non-critical cached DEKs we can continue serving but with elevated alerts and limited TTL. for high-availability we recommend a multi-zone HSM cluster or a secondary wrap key escrow we manage with strict controls.
10:52 Aisha: escrow — that sounds worrying; how do you protect escrowed keys?
11:05 Diego: escrowed keys are wrapped with a secondary protection key stored in an HSM with dual-control. we support split-knowledge where two operators must authorize extraction. the escrow process is auditable and we can provide documentation for legal review.
11:28 Liam: about performance — have you benchmarked wrap/unwrap rates for common HSM vendors? we need numbers because our billing depends on ops.
11:40 Diego: yes, we have a benchmarks sheet; we'll share numbers for AWS CloudHSM and common appliances. note that wrap/unwrap ops are relatively cheap if you avoid doing them per token; the design tries to amortize cost via DEK caching and lazy rewrap.
12:05 Maya: competition — any reason you'd pick CloudAI or InferX here?
12:15 Aisha: we looked at CloudAI but they're less flexible for BYOK and InferX pricing for HSM ops was unclear. performance was ok but their audit trail story wasn't as mature.
12:28 Diego: ok noted.

12:40 Aisha: quick operational question — how are key rotations communicated? we need rotation events to be in our change log and we require a signed attestation per rotation.
12:52 Diego: rotations generate an auditable event with a signature; we can ship rotation manifests and hook a webhook to your change log system.
13:05 Sofia: any special legal language re: key custody? procurement will ask for a clause that keys never leave customer territory for EU.
13:18 Maya: for private deployments/DEDICATED we can include a clause limiting processing to EU regions and attest to key residency, we'll work with legal.
13:32 Liam: let's talk POC scope — we want encrypted log ingestion of a subset of production events (PII masked) into our SIEM, with BYOK where the wrap key stays in our HSM, and a proof-of-concept of signed daily manifests.
13:48 Diego: great scope — that maps to a 2-week POC: day 1 onboarding and key ceremony, day 3 integration to SIEM, day 7 sign & verify daily manifests, day 10 load test, wrap-up.
14:05 Maya: ok let's wrap — recap of next steps and who does what.
